A 1 V source drives a series LCR loop: what does a meter read across each part?

Listen to the intro

About: peak potential differences across R, L, C, and L with C, in a driven series LCR circuit

About this simulation

On screen
A graph of the meter's peak reading against the source's angular frequency ω, 0 to 20 × 103 rad/s and 0 to 6 V, with a dashed line at the source amplitude V0 and a thin dashed line at ω0 = 104 rad/s. Each meter position keeps its own coloured curve over the range swept in that position; a dot marks the present ω. Curves of the previous resistance are kept in grey. The inset shows the circuit with the meter's leads across the components of the present position, drawn in that position's colour, and the reading on its dial. In questions 2 to 5 the dial, and the present curve and dot, stay covered until you answer.
Controls
The ω slider sweeps the source's angular frequency from 500 to 20 000 rad/s in steps of 50 rad/s and fills in the curve of the present meter position; the box beside it takes an exact value. The resistance buttons choose R = 20, 50 or 100 Ω; the old curves turn grey and fresh ones start. The meter buttons connect the voltmeter across R, across L, across C, or across L and C together; all curves are kept.
Readouts
In the sidebar, below the controls: ω, the resonant angular frequency ω0 = 1/√(LC) and the quality factor Q = ω0L/R; then, from question 6 on and in free exploration, the meter reading and the peak current I0.
Model
Steady state only, ideal components, source amplitude V0 = 1.00 V (peak), L = 10 mH, C = 1 µF. The meter reads the peak amplitude, not the rms: the peak current V0/Z times the resistance, the reactance ωL or 1/ωC, or the net reactance |ωL − 1/ωC| across L and C together. A real meter would usually read rms, 1/√2 of these.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Sweep with the meter on R

Set R = 20 Ω, connect the meter across R and set ω = 2000 rad/s. Before sweeping, predict the largest reading of the meter as you sweep ω up to 20 000 rad/s, and where it comes. Then sweep.

2 · Across C at resonance

Keep R = 20 Ω, set ω = 10 000 rad/s, which is ω0, and connect the meter across C. Before looking at the reading, predict it.

3 · Across L at resonance

Keep the settings of question 2 and move the meter across L. Before looking at the reading, predict it.

4 · Across L and C together

Keep the settings of question 3 and move the meter across L and C together. Before looking at the reading, predict it.

5 · A larger resistance

Set R = 50 Ω, keep ω = 10 000 rad/s and connect the meter across C. Before looking at the reading, predict it.

6 · Where the capacitor peaks

Set R = 100 Ω, so that Q = 1, keep the meter across C and set ω = 500 rad/s. Before sweeping up to 20 000 rad/s, predict where the reading is largest. Then sweep.

7 · What you found

At ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 10 000 rad/s the potential differences across L and C are equal in size and opposite in phase, so together they read zero and the resistor takes the whole source amplitude V0 = 1.00 V.

Each of them alone reads ω0LV0/R = QV0: 5.00 V with R = 20 Ω and 2.00 V with R = 50 Ω, far more than the source. When Q is small the peaks move apart: with Q = 1 the capacitor's reading peaks at 1.15 V near 7 000 rad/s, below ω0, and the inductor's near 14 000 rad/s, above it.

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A voltmeter across one part of a driven series LCR circuit does not read the source. It reads the current through that part times the part's own impedance, and the current depends on the frequency. The sim sweeps the source's angular frequency ω and plots the meter's peak reading for four positions of the meter.

What you'll learn

  • Why a reading depends on which part the meter is across, and on ω.
  • What the resonant angular frequency ω0 does to the current.
  • What the quality factor 𝒬 measures, and how R sets it.
  • Where each reading is largest as ω is swept.
The sim's two views: the graph of readings, and the circuit with the meter.

What's on screen

  • Green curve: the peak reading with the meter across R.
  • Red curve: across L.
  • Blue curve: across C.
  • Violet curve: across L and C together.
  • Dashed lines: the source amplitude V0 = 1.00 V, and ω0 = 10 000 rad/s. A dot marks the present ω.
  • Grey curves: the previous R. The inset shows the circuit and the meter's dial.
See itLook at the graph, the circuit inset and the Readouts panel. Watch for: the meter across R, reading 0.04 V at ω = 2000 rad/s, with the dashed lines at V₀ and ω₀.

The model is fixed: steady state, ideal parts, V0 = 1.00 V (peak), L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF. The meter reads the peak, not the rms; a real meter would usually show 1/√2 of these.

03

At resonance the impedance is just R, and the resistor reads V₀

The three parts carry the same current and their impedances add (notes, section 7.6). The peak current is largest when |Z| is smallest.

Eqs. (7.73) and (7.74) with I0 = V0/|Z|.

That is when ωL = 1/ωC, at ω0 = 1/√(LC). With L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF, ω0 = 10 000 rad/s, and ωL and 1/ωC are both 100 Ω. They cancel, the current is in phase with the source, and the resistor reads R I0 = V0 = 1.00 V whatever R is.

Eq. (7.76) and the values at resonance.
The resistor reading for R = 20, 50 and 100 Ω. A smaller R gives a narrower peak, but every peak is 1.00 V.

Away from ω0 the impedance is larger, so the current and the resistor's reading are smaller, falling towards zero at both ends of the sweep.

See itSet R = 20 Ω, put the meter across R and move ω to 10 000 rad/s. Watch for: the green curve peaking at 1.00 V exactly at ω₀, where the peak current is at its largest, 50.0 mA.
04

The inductor and capacitor each read 𝒬 V₀ at resonance

At ω0 the reactances are not zero. They are equal, 100 Ω each, and the current is V0/R. So the potential difference across each is ω0L I0, which is 𝒬 times the source (notes, Problem 2 of section 7.6):

The quality factor and the readings at resonance.

For R = 20 Ω, 𝒬 = 5: the current is 50 mA, and the inductor and the capacitor read 5.00 V each, five times the source. The notes remark that this can be much larger than V0 when ω0L ≫ R.

Phasors at ω0 for R = 20 Ω. VL is a quarter turn ahead of the current, VC a quarter turn behind.
See itKeep R = 20 Ω, put the meter across C at ω₀, then across L. Watch for: 5.00 V across C, then 5.00 V across L, with 𝒬 = 5.00 and the peak current at 50.0 mA.
05

The inductor and capacitor together read zero at resonance

The meter across L and C together reads the difference of their potential differences, never the sum. With i = I0 cos ωt the inductor has vL = −ωL I0 sin ωt and the capacitor vC = (I0/ωC) sin ωt, opposite in sign at every instant:

The ratio of the two, and the pair's reading.

At ω0 the factor is −1: the two cancel at every instant, so the pair reads 0.00 V while each reads 5.00 V alone. The source then drives the current through R alone, and V0 = VR.

One period at ω0 for R = 20 Ω: vL and vC mirror each other, and their sum is zero.

Away from ω0 they do not cancel. For R = 20 Ω the pair reads 1.00 V at 500 rad/s and 0.99 V at 20 000 rad/s: nearly the whole source, since the current is small and R takes almost none of it.

See itPut the meter across L and C together at ω₀, with R = 20 Ω. Watch for: the violet curve falling to 0.00 V at ω₀, and the one-period panel with the red and blue traces mirroring each other.
06

A larger resistance lowers 𝒬 and the readings

𝒬 = ω0L/R, so R = 20, 50 and 100 Ω give 𝒬 = 5, 2 and 1. At ω0 the resistor still reads V0 for each: the current falls as 1/R while the resistance rises as R. The capacitor reads 𝒬 V0:

The capacitor reading at ω0: 5.00, 2.00 and 1.00 V.

With R = 50 Ω the peak current at ω0 is 20 mA, and the capacitor reads 2.00 V. The notes also write 𝒬 = ω0/Δω, where Δω = R/L is the full width of the power resonance: a smaller R gives a sharper peak and a larger 𝒬.

See itKeep the meter across C at ω₀ and step R from 20 to 50 to 100 Ω. Watch for: the capacitor reading falling from 5.00 to 2.00 to 1.00 V, with the earlier curve turning grey at each step.
07

The capacitor's peak lies below ω₀

The current peaks at ω0, but the capacitor reads I0/ωC, and the 1/ω keeps growing as ω falls. That pulls the capacitor's maximum below ω0. The notes (Problem 1 of section 7.6) give where it is, provided γ² < 2ω0², that is 𝒬 > 0.71; substituting gives the peak value:

The capacitor's maximum, with γ = R/L. The value follows by substituting the angular frequency.
R = 100 Ω, so 𝒬 = 1. The capacitor peaks below ω0 and the inductor above it.

For 𝒬 = 1 the peak is at ω0/√2 = 7071 rad/s and reads 1.15 V. For 𝒬 = 2 it is at 9354 rad/s (2.07 V), and for 𝒬 = 5 at 9899 rad/s (5.03 V): a slight shift when 𝒬 is large. The inductor's curve is the mirror: at 𝒬 = 1 it peaks at √2 ω0 with the same height. That follows by the same method; it is not in the notes. The slider steps in 50 rad/s, so it reaches 7050 and 14 150.

See itSet R = 100 Ω, so 𝒬 = 1, with the meter across C, and set ω to 7050 rad/s. Watch for: the blue curve at 1.15 V, above V₀ and left of ω₀, and the red curve peaking at the same height to the right.
08

Where it matters

  • Tuning a radio. The aerial picks up small voltages at many frequencies. A resonant circuit whose capacitance is adjusted to bring ω0 to the chosen station responds strongly to that station and weakly to the others (notes, section 7.6).
  • Voltages larger than the source. In a circuit with a large 𝒬 the inductor and the capacitor each take 𝒬 V0, so a capacitor in a tuned circuit must stand far more than the source's amplitude.
  • Sharp or broad. 𝒬 = ω0/Δω says how narrow the resonance is. R = 20 Ω gives a width of 2000 rad/s, and R = 100 Ω gives 10 000 rad/s.
Go deeper: the width of the resonance

The mean power is ⟨𝒫⟩ = V0²R / 2[R² + (ωL − 1/ωC)²] (7.77), largest at ω0. It falls to half when ωL − 1/ωC = ±R, and the two angular frequencies are ω± = √(ω0² + γ²/4) ± γ/2 (7.79). Their separation is Δω = R/L exactly (7.80), so 𝒬 = ω0/Δω = ω0L/R (7.81). The sim shows amplitudes of potential difference, not power.

09

Summary

In one line. A meter across one part of a driven series LCR circuit reads the current through that part times its own impedance, and the current depends on the frequency.
  • At ω0 = 1/√(LC) = 10 000 rad/s, Z = R, I0 = V0/R, and the resistor reads V0 = 1.00 V for every R.
  • There L and C each read 𝒬 V0 (𝒬 = ω0L/R = 5, 2, 1), and the pair reads 0.00 V because vL = −(ω/ω0)² vC.
  • The capacitor's peak is at ω² = ω0² − γ²/2, below ω0: 7071 rad/s and 1.15 V at 𝒬 = 1.

Common mix-ups

  • "At resonance the capacitor reads nothing, because the reactances cancel." They cancel in the loop; each alone reads 5.00 V at 𝒬 = 5.
  • "The capacitor's curve peaks at ω0, with the current." The current does. The capacitor's extra 1/ω moves its peak below ω0.
  • "Raising R lowers the resistor's reading at ω0." The current falls as 1/R and the resistance rises as R, so it stays at V0 = 1.00 V.

Things to try on your own

  • R = 50 Ω, ω = 10 000 rad/s, meter across L: it should read 2.00 V, and across L and C 0.00 V.
  • R = 20 Ω, meter across C: the largest reading is 5.03 V at 9900 rad/s, just below ω0.
